The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

derivations.claim: Put $\rho(dt)=t^{-1}e^{-t}dt$ on $(0,\infty)$; [F22] makes this a measure with a nonnegative density, relative to Lebesgue measure, and partition the mark axis into $I_0=[1,\infty)$ and $I_m=[1/(m+1),1/m)$ for $m\ge1$. These disjoint strips cover $(0,\infty)$. For $m\ge1$, $\rho(I_m)\le 1/m$ because $t^{-1}\le m+1$ and $e^{-t}\le1$ there, while $\rho(I_m)\ge1/(e(m+1))>0$ because $t^{-1}\ge m$, $e^{-t}\ge e^{-1}$, and the interval length is $1/(m(m+1))$. Also $\rho(I_0)\le\int_1^\infty e^{-t}dt<\infty$ and $\rho(I_0)\ge e^{-2}/2>0$ by restricting to $[1,2]$. Thus every strip has finite positive mass. By [F3] and [F14], $\mu=\alpha\otimes\rho$ is sigma-finite and $\mu_m:=\mu|_{\mathsf X\times I_m}$ has finite positive total $\lambda_m=\alpha(\mathsf X)\rho(I_m)$. Let $Q_m=\mu_m/\lambda_m$.

Index count coordinates by $m\ge0$ and mark coordinates by $(m,\ell)$ with $m\ge0,\ell\ge1$. Their spaces are $\mathbb N_0$ and $\mathsf X\times(0,\infty)$, respectively, hence standard Borel by [F1], [F21], and [F23]. Assign every finite set of coordinates the product of the laws $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_m)$ and $Q_m$. These finite-dimensional laws are consistent because coordinate projections of a finite product recover the corresponding marginal products. By [F1] and [A1] they extend to one probability law. The product rectangle formula gives mutual independence of each finite coordinate family by [F20], and [F13] identifies its joint law with the product. Thus it supports mutually independent $N_m\sim \operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_m)$ and $Z_{m\ell}=(X_{m\ell},T_{m\ell})\sim Q_m$.

Define $N=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{\ell\le N_m\}}\delta_{Z_{m\ell}}$. Each $N_m$ is finite, so this is a countable sum of Dirac measures and is a counting measure by [F8]. For every measurable $B$, its evaluation is the increasing limit of finite sums of measurable functions of the coordinates; hence $N(B)$ is measurable. Thus $N$ is a random counting measure.

Fix pairwise-disjoint measurable sets $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ with $\mu(B_j)<\infty$. Within strip $m$, put $q_{jm}=Q_m(B_j)$ and $q_{0m}=1-\sum_{j=1}^r q_{jm}$. Conditional on $N_m=n$, independent marks assign counts $(k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ with $n=k_0+\cdots+k_r$. There are $n!/\prod_{j=0}^r k_j!$ assignments of the $n$ mark indices to these cells, and each assignment has probability $\prod_{j=0}^r q_{jm}^{k_j}$, so the count vector has mass $n!\prod_{j=0}^r q_{jm}^{k_j}/\prod_{j=0}^r k_j!$ (with $0^0=1$). Summing over $k_0$ and using the Poisson mass in [F2] gives $\Pr\{N_m(B_j)=k_j,\ 1\le j\le r\}=e^{-\lambda_m}\bigl(\prod_{j=1}^r(\lambda_mq_{jm})^{k_j}/k_j!\bigr)e^{\lambda_mq_{0m}}=\prod_{j=1}^r e^{-\mu_m(B_j)}\mu_m(B_j)^{k_j}/k_j!$; here $\lambda_mq_{jm}=\mu_m(B_j)$ and $\lambda_m(1-q_{0m})=\sum_j\mu_m(B_j)$. Thus the strip counts are independent Poisson variables with means $\mu_m(B_j)$. The series over $k_0$ is the exponential series [F17].

Define $\Gamma(A)=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{\ell\ge1} \mathbf1_{\{\ell\le N_m\}}T_{m\ell}\mathbf1_{\{X_{m\ell}\in A\}}$ for $A\in\mathcal A$. This is a measurable nonnegative weighted sum of Dirac measures, hence a measure by [F8]. For each strip, independence of $N_m$ and its marks [F13], expectation against their law [F11], and $\mathbb E N_m=\lambda_m$ from [F2] give $\mathbb E\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_m}T_{m\ell}\mathbf1_{\{X_{m\ell}\in A\}} =\lambda_m\int t\mathbf1_A(x)\,Q_m(dx,dt) =\int_{A\times I_m}t\,\mu(dx,dt)$. Monotone convergence [F16] then gives $\mathbb E\Gamma(A)=\sum_m\int_{A\times I_m}t\,\mu(dx,dt) =\alpha(A)\int_0^\infty e^{-t}dt=\alpha(A)$ by [F3] and [F6].

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and choose $|u_j|<\delta<1$. On strip $m$, define $g_m(x,t)=\sum_{j=1}^r e^{u_jt}\mathbf1_{A_j}(x) +\mathbf1_{\mathsf X\setminus\cup_jA_j}(x)$. Conditional on $N_m=n$, the independent marks give the exponential factor $(\int g_m\,dQ_m)^n$. Summing its Poisson series yields $\mathbb E\exp(\sum_j u_j\Gamma_M(A_j)) =\exp(\sum_j\alpha(A_j)\int_{\cup_{m\le M}I_m} (e^{u_jt}-1)\rho(dt))$, where $\Gamma_M$ sums the first $M+1$ strips. The mark integral is finite on each strip because the strips are bounded away from zero and $u_j<1$; the Poisson series is [F17].

For each finite $M$, the sums over $m\le M$ are independent Poisson counts: convolution and [F18] give $\sum_{h=0}^k e^{-a}a^h/h!\,e^{-b}b^{k-h}/(k-h)! =e^{-(a+b)}(a+b)^k/k!$, and iteration handles $M$. By [F16], their increasing total counts have $\mathbb E N(B_j)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\sum_{m\le M}\mu_m(B_j)=\mu(B_j)<\infty$. Thus the full counts are finite almost surely and the truncated integer counts eventually stabilize. Their joint point probabilities converge both to the point probabilities of the full count vector (by eventual stabilization) and to the product Poisson masses with means $\mu(B_j)$ (by continuity of the Poisson mass formula in its mean). Hence the full counts are independent Poisson variables with means $\mu(B_j)$. Therefore $N$ satisfies [[def-poisson-random-measure]].

Since $\mathbb E\Gamma(\mathsf X)=\alpha(\mathsf X)<\infty$, $\Gamma(\mathsf X)<\infty$ almost surely: if it were infinite on a set of positive probability, its expectation would exceed every finite bound. Also, $\Gamma(A)$ is measurable for every $A$ as a monotone limit of finite coordinate sums.

For $u<1$, $\int_0^\infty(e^{ut}-1)t^{-1}e^{-t}dt =\int_0^u(1-v)^{-1}dv=-\log(1-u)$: use $(e^{ut}-1)/t=\int_0^u e^{vt}dv$, Tonelli on the positive or negative part, and [F6]. In particular $\mathbb E e^{\delta\Gamma(\mathsf X)} =(1-\delta)^{-\alpha(\mathsf X)}<\infty$, by monotone convergence [F16] on the nonnegative truncations. Let $J_+=\{j: \alpha(A_j)>0\}$. For $j\in J_+$, [F4], [F5], and the Euler integral [F19], with $t=(1-u)y$, give $\mathbb E e^{uY}=\Gamma(a)^{-1}\int_0^\infty y^{a-1}e^{-(1-u)y}dy=(1-u)^{-a}$ for $Y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,1)$ and $u<1$.
